name: Magnesium malate
lead: Magnesium malate is the magnesium salt of malic acid, sold as a mineral supplement [1]. Wikipedia notes it is discussed as more bioavailable than citrate or glycinate, citing a single supplier source [1]. Supplement sellers also promote it for muscle soreness, exercise recovery and fibromyalgia pain [2].

The European Food Safety Authority has evaluated di-magnesium malate as a novel food ingredient and magnesium source [3]. Human studies directly testing the malate form for appearance or performance are scarce in the sources reviewed.
infobox: EFSA evaluation of di-magnesium malate as novel food [3]

paras: It is used to supply magnesium for deficiency from low intake, malabsorption or conditions such as diabetes and chronic diarrhoea, and supplier materials claim benefits for pain and exercise recovery [2].
Two 2019 studies compared the bioavailability and dose-dependent absorption of different magnesium compounds [4][5]; magnesium malate is not singled out in the abstracts available here.

Reference text says small trials in fibromyalgia reported reduced pain and tenderness and that athletes showed less muscle soreness, but these are secondary summaries without cited trial details here [2]. No studies of the malate form for physique or appearance outcomes were found. A registered trial of a magnesium complex on body composition in students has been listed [6].
EFSA evaluated the compound for use in foods, supplements and total diet replacement [3].

card.summary: Magnesium bound to malic acid, pitched for energy, soreness and fibromyalgia; direct human evidence is thin.
card.note: Bioavailability superiority claims rest on supplier sources.

quick.overview:
Magnesium malate pairs magnesium with malic acid and is sold to correct deficiency and for muscle soreness and recovery.

Claims of better absorption come from a supplier source; EFSA has evaluated it as a food ingredient.
quick.mechanism: It supplies magnesium, which is involved in muscle and nerve function; malate is an intermediate in energy metabolism, which sellers cite for energy claims.
quick.risks: Human safety data specific to this form are limited in the sources; EFSA assessed its use in foods and supplements.
